questions.q: In which of these is the final c silent?
questions.why: c is one of the CaReFuL consonants that usually survive at the end of a word, but le banc is one of the words that breaks the tendency: it ends on a nasal vowel with no k.

questions.q: Which of these words keeps its final r?
questions.why: Every -er infinitive ends in the sound of é: parler, manger, travailler. Short -er words keep the r instead: la mer, hier, l'hiver, le fer, cher.

questions.q: The mnemonic CaReFuL tells you which final consonants often stay audible. Which letters is it standing for?
questions.why: It is a tendency, not a law: le tabac, gentil, le fusil and the whole -er infinitive family all break it. Everything else final is silent by default.

questions.q: In which of these is the ending -ent actually pronounced?
questions.why: The silence belongs to the verb ending, not to the letters. On a third person plural verb, -ent is completely silent; in an ordinary word like souvent, content or le vent it is a nasal vowel.

questions.q: What is the audible difference between « le gâteau » and « les gâteaux » ?
choices: Only the article: the noun sounds identical
The x is heard at the end of the plural
The plural has an extra syllable
There is no difference at all
questions.why: Plural -s and -x are never pronounced, so the whole singular/plural distinction rides on the article. If you blur le and les, or un and des, your listener cannot tell how many you mean.

questions.q: What sound does the ending -ée have in « l'année » or « la durée » ?
questions.why: A vowel followed by a silent e keeps its own sound: -ée is é, -ie is "ee" (la vie), -oue is "oo" (la roue). The e adds nothing but a letter.

questions.q: « grand » ends on a nasal vowel with no d. Write the form with a silent final e, where the d becomes audible.
questions.why: The job of a silent final e is to make the consonant before it sound. Il est grand and elle est grande differ by exactly that one consonant.

questions.q: « heureux » ends in a silent x. Write the form ending in -euse, where that letter is heard as a z.
questions.why: Same mechanism as grand/grande: français becomes française with an audible z, vert becomes verte with an audible t.

questions.q: Write the ils / elles form of « chanter ».
questions.why: Written with four extra letters, said exactly like je chante, tu chantes and il chante. Three of the six present-tense forms of an -er verb are homophones.

questions.q: Write the vous form of « chanter ».
questions.why: -ez is the sound of é, like the infinitive. Only nous (-ons) and vous (-ez) break away from the silent block of the other four forms.

questions.q: Type what you hear, singular or plural.
questions.why: The noun is identical in both numbers; only the vowel of the article tells you. les is a tight "lay", le is a soft "luh".

questions.q: Say this out loud. The last four letters are silent.
questions.why: Verb -ent is silent, so this sounds exactly like il parle. Only the pronoun tells a listener how many people are talking.

questions.q: Say this out loud, and land clearly on the final consonant.
questions.why: Swallow the d and you have said elle est grand. In speech the audible final consonant is the agreement.

questions.q: Say this at natural speed — the e in the middle usually disappears.
questions.why: An unaccented e inside a word is routinely dropped: maintenant is two syllables in ordinary speech, la semaine can lose its first e, and je ne sais pas collapses almost to one word.

questions.q: A final -e is silent. Explain why it still matters, with two examples.
a: Its job is to make the consonant before it audible: grand has no d but grande does, petit has no t but petite does, français ends in a vowel but française ends in a z sound. That is the whole mechanism behind feminine adjectives and past participles, so swallowing the final consonant removes the agreement from your speech.
questions.why: Almost every audible masculine/feminine contrast in French comes from this one spelling fact.
